title: Requirements & Architecture
description: Review of firmware requirements, architecture, resource budgets, third-party code and, where it applies, functional safety.

items.text: Firmware requirements are written down and traced to the product and EE requirements
items.hint: Each firmware requirement should name its parent (a system or EE requirement) so a change upstream shows what it touches.

items.text: Every requirement has a verification method (test, analysis, inspection or demonstration)
items.hint: Use the Requirements tab: a requirement with no way to verify it can't be signed off.

items.text: Timing requirements are quantified (latency, response time, update rates)
items.hint: "Fast" isn't testable. E.g. "relay off within 100 ms of a fault" or "display update within 50 ms of a touch".

items.text: Behavior on power-up, reset and power loss is specified
items.hint: What state are outputs in during boot? What is restored after a power cut, and what is lost?

items.text: Error and fault behavior is specified, not just the happy path
items.hint: List the faults the firmware must detect (sensor open or short, comms loss, storage full) and what it does for each.

items.text: User-visible behavior (UI flows, LEDs, error codes) has a spec the product owner agreed to
items.hint: Error codes and LED patterns end up in manuals and support scripts. Freeze them deliberately.

items.text: Regulatory and certification requirements that land on firmware are identified
items.hint: E.g. radio duty cycle and region settings, IEC 60730 class B self-tests, EN 18031 / RED cybersecurity, IEC 62304.

items.text: An architecture document shows the layers, modules and their dependencies
items.hint: A one-page block diagram is enough: HAL, drivers, middleware, application, and which way calls go.

items.text: The hardware abstraction is separated from application logic
items.hint: Application code that touches registers directly can't be unit tested off target or ported to the next MCU.

items.text: Flash, RAM and CPU budgets exist, with margin for the product's life
items.hint: Plan to ship with at least 25–30% free flash and RAM so field updates have room to grow.

items.text: The execution model is chosen and justified (superloop, RTOS, event-driven)
items.hint: Record why. The choice drives timing analysis, testing and power management.

items.text: The partition between processors is defined where there is more than one
items.hint: Who owns which peripheral, how they talk, and how one updates or resets the other.

items.text: State machines for the main modes are drawn and match the code
items.hint: Modes such as boot, setup, run, fault and update. Unhandled event/state pairs are a common source of field bugs.

items.text: Configuration is separated from code (build variants, region, SKU)
items.hint: Prefer one image with runtime configuration, or a small, named set of build variants.

items.text: Every third-party component is listed with version, source and license
items.hint: SDKs, RTOS, stacks, libraries, vendor examples. This becomes the SBOM.

items.text: Licenses are compatible with how the product ships
items.hint: GPL and LGPL components have obligations for linked, distributed binaries. Check with the client before shipping them.

items.text: Vendor SDK and stack versions are pinned, and the update policy is written down
items.hint: Pin by version or commit. Unpinned SDK updates change behavior between builds.

items.text: Local modifications to third-party code are kept as patches
items.hint: So they can be re-applied when the upstream version changes.

items.text: The applicable safety standard and software class are identified
items.hint: E.g. IEC 60730 class B for appliance controls, IEC 61508 SIL, IEC 62304 class A/B/C for medical.

items.text: A hazard analysis identifies the firmware's contribution to each hazard
items.hint: Each hazard the firmware can cause or must prevent, with the mitigation and how it's verified.

items.text: Safety functions are isolated from non-safety code
items.hint: Separate tasks or partitions, MPU regions, or a separate processor, so a bug elsewhere can't defeat them.

items.text: Required self-tests are implemented (CPU, RAM, flash CRC, clock)
items.hint: IEC 60730 class B lists the self-tests by component. Vendor class B libraries cover most of them.

items.text: Software of unknown provenance (SOUP) is listed with its risk assessment
items.hint: IEC 62304 asks for each SOUP item's requirements and known anomalies.
